title: Quantum memory advantage for quantum process tomography
authors: Carlos Bravo-Prieto, Weiyuan Gong, Antonio Anna Mele
abstract: Quantum process tomography, the task of learning an unknown quantum channel from black-box access, is a central problem in quantum information. In this setting, protocols with quantum memory can coherently store and jointly process quantum information obtained from multiple channel uses, whereas protocols without quantum memory must measure after each use and retain only a classical transcript of the measurement outcomes. A fundamental open question is whether quantum memory provides a query-complexity advantage even when protocols without quantum memory may adapt their experiments based on all previous outcomes with unbounded classical computational power. In this work, we show that it does. We determine the optimal query complexity of quantum process tomography without quantum memory up to a constant factor to be $Θ(d_{\mathrm{in}}^3 d_{\mathrm{out}}^3/\varepsilon^2)$, where $d_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $d_{\mathrm{out}}$ are the channel input and output dimensions, respectively, and $\varepsilon$ is the target diamond-norm accuracy. More precisely, we prove that any incoherent protocol for this task, including adaptive protocols, requires $Ω(d_{\mathrm{in}}^3 d_{\mathrm{out}}^3/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, even when each channel use may be assisted by arbitrary fresh ancilla, and we present a non-adaptive, ancilla-free incoherent protocol achieving the matching upper bound $O(d_{\mathrm{in}}^3 d_{\mathrm{out}}^3/\varepsilon^2)$. Our results thereby generalize the optimal sample-complexity bounds for single-copy state tomography, recovered as the special case $d_{\mathrm{in}}=1$. By contrast, coherent protocols with quantum memory achieve query complexity $Θ(d_{\mathrm{in}}^2 d_{\mathrm{out}}^2/\varepsilon^2)$. Hence, our results establish a rigorous learning separation between quantum process tomography with and without quantum memory.
summary: This paper rigorously proves that utilizing quantum memory offers a significant computational advantage in Quantum Process Tomography (QPT). It establishes that protocols without memory require query complexity scaling as $d_{in}^3 d_{out}^3/\varepsilon^2$, while those with memory achieve a much better scaling of $d_{in}^2 d_{out}^2/\varepsilon^2$. This separation quantifies the necessity and power of quantum coherence in characterizing unknown quantum channels.
main_problem: The central problem is Quantum Process Tomography (QPT): learning an unknown quantum channel from black-box access.
main_result: The paper establishes a rigorous separation between QPT protocols with and without quantum memory, showing that the required query complexity scales differently in both cases.
method: The authors use information-theoretic techniques, constructing local families of channels to derive lower bounds on sample complexity, which are matched by non-adaptive upper bounds.
model_or_system: The model involves an unknown quantum channel $\Phi: \mathcal{L}(A) 	o \mathcal{L}(B)$ acting between finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces $A$ and $B$. The comparison is drawn between protocols that use memory (coherent) versus those that reset after each measurement (incoherent).
key_observables: The estimation error is measured in the diamond norm ($\|\cdot\|_{\diamond}$), and the complexity is quantified by the required number of queries ($T$).
important_parameters: Dimensions $d_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $d_{\mathrm{out}}$, and the target accuracy $\varepsilon$. The scaling difference between memory-assisted ($\Theta(d_{in}^2 d_{out}^2/\varepsilon^2)$) and non-memory protocols ($\Theta(d_{in}^3 d_{out}^3/\varepsilon^2)$) is key.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and focuses on classical adaptivity for the incoherent case, while the coherent case utilizes quantum memory.
figures_summary: Figure 1 provides an overview of the proof strategy, linking local channel families to single-round testers and culminating in a likelihood-ratio estimate leading to the lower bound $T = \Omega(d_{in}^3 d_{out}^3 / \epsilon^2)$.
paper_structure: The paper develops necessary mathematical tools (e.g., random-basis reconstruction, concentration inequalities) before applying them to establish a lower bound for adaptive incoherent protocols, which is then matched by an upper bound.
why_interesting: This work provides fundamental resource quantification for quantum characterization tasks, directly impacting the feasibility limits of experimental quantum computing hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of the proof strategy. We first construct a local family of channels near the completely depolarizing channel. Each channel is indexed by a matrix perturbation of the normalized Choi operator. We then represent every round of an adaptive incoherent protocol by a single-round tester. Along any transcript, the adaptivity protocol yields a deterministic sequence of tester elements.
